title: Where are you from, what do you do
goal: Say where you're from, your nationality, and your job — and understand why one word can change shape three times depending on who you're talking about.
bekal: ask and answer about origin, nationality, and job
make nationality adjectives yourself from country names
negate sentences without a verb using مش

dialogs.title: حوار — في استراحة المعهد
dialogs.intro: First break. Budi gets a tea at the institute cafeteria, and a female student says hello.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: Hi! You're the new student, right?

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: I'm Mona. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: إندونيسي؟ جميل أوي! وانت بتشتغل إيه؟
lines.id: Indonesian? How lovely! And what do you do?
lines.literal: Indonesian? beautiful very! and you you-work what?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أنا مهندس، بس دلوقتي أنا طالب هنا.
lines.baca: ana muhandis, bas dilwa’ti ana ṭaalib hina.
lines.id: I'm an engineer, but right now I'm a student here.
lines.literal: I engineer, but now I student here.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: And how long have you been here?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: من أسبوع بس. لسه جديد أوي.
lines.id: Just a week. I'm still very new.
lines.literal: from week only. still new very.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: لأ، هما في إندونيسيا. أنا لوحدي.
lines.baca: la’, humma fi Indunisya. ana liwahdi.
lines.id: No, they're in Indonesia. I'm on my own.
lines.literal: no, they in Indonesia. I by-myself.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: معلش. مصر بلد كبيرة وأهلها طيبين.
lines.baca: ma‘lesh. Maṣr balad kibiira wi ahlaha ṭayyibiin.
lines.id: Hang in there. Egypt is a big country and its people are kind.
lines.literal: never-mind. Egypt country big and its-people kind.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أيوه، حاسس بكده. وانتي منين في مصر؟
lines.baca: aywa, haasis bikida. w inti minēn fi Maṣr?
lines.id: Yes, I can feel that. And where in Egypt are you from?
lines.literal: yes, feeling with-that. and you(f) from-where in Egypt?

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: أنا من أسوان، بس ساكنة في القاهرة.
lines.baca: ana min Aswaan, bas sakna fil-Qaahira.
lines.id: I'm from Aswan, but I live in Cairo.
lines.literal: I from Aswan, but living(f) in Cairo.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: بعيدة شوية، بس حلوة أوي. لازم تزورها.
lines.baca: bi‘iida shuwayya, bas hilwa ’awi. laazim tizurha.
lines.id: A bit far, but really beautiful. You have to visit it.
lines.literal: far a-little, but sweet very. must you-visit-it.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: إن شاء الله. الفرصة سعيدة يا منى.
lines.id: God willing. Nice to meet you, Mona.

notes: **The word منين combines من and فين.** Literally "from where", and like every Egyptian question word it sits at the end: انت منين؟ In Fusha the same sentence is مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ, in reverse order.

**The word صح works like "right?" in English.** Tack it onto the end of a sentence to ask for agreement. Its twin is مش كده؟, literally "not like that?" — like "isn't it?" — and the two are interchangeable.

**Country names become adjectives by adding ـي.** مصر becomes مصري *maṣri*, لبنان becomes لبناني *libnaani*, إندونيسيا becomes إندونيسي *indunisi*. For a woman add ـة; for a group of people add ـين. You may know this ending from English words like *Iraqi*, *Saudi*, or *Pakistani*.

**The word دلوقتي means "now", and it's typically Egyptian.** The Fusha الآن is hardly ever heard in conversation. It comes from دي الوقت — literally "this time" — which gradually fused into one word.

**The word لوحدي means "on my own", and it changes with the person.** لوحدي *liwahdi* for me, لوحدك *liwahdak* for you, لوحده *liwahdu* for him. The ending attached here is exactly the same as the possessive ending.

**Note ساكنة, not بتسكن.** For living somewhere, sitting, standing, carrying, and knowing, Egyptian prefers an active participle (a verbal adjective) over a verb. This important feature is covered in full in unit 17; for now just learn it as it is.

grammars.title: From country name to nationality adjective
body: Egyptian makes nationality words with one recipe that has almost no exceptions: drop a final ـا from the country name if there is one, then add ـي.
after: The last two rows are irregular, and both are among the most frequently used words — so learn them as they are. Their plurals are أمريكان and إنجليز, not forms ending in ـين.
The nationality adjective also serves as the name of the language, with الـ in front: العربي *il-‘arabi* (Arabic), الإنجليزي *il-ingliizi* (English), الإندونيسي *il-indunisi* (Indonesian).
Notice that **أنا مصري** means "I'm Egyptian", while **أنا من مصر** means "I'm from Egypt". Both are correct, and Egyptians use them interchangeably.

grammars.title: The word مش — one word for every non-verb negation
body: The word مش goes right in front of the part being negated. It never changes form, whether masculine, feminine, singular, or plural.
after: Notice that this one word مش covers both "not" with nouns and "not" with adjectives — and even "don't" with words like فاهم. Egyptian makes no distinction.
What is **not** negated with مش is a verb marked with بـ. For that there's the wrapper مـ...ـش, covered in full in unit 10 — for example مابشتغلش *mabashtaghalsh* (I don't work).

blocks.text: There are two ways to ask someone's job, and both are equally common: انت بتشتغل إيه؟ *inta bitishtaghal ’ēh?* ("what do you work?") and انت شغلك إيه؟ *inta shughlak ’ēh?* ("your job what?"). The second is a little more casual.

blocks.title: Titles used to address people
items: The word أستاذ *ustaaz* is used for any adult man, not just teachers — much like "sir" or "Mr." in English. Its feminine form أستاذة *ustaaza* works like "ma'am".
The word دكتور is used for medical doctors and for university lecturers with a PhD. In Egypt the title is used with pride and never skipped.
The word مدام *madaam* is for a married woman and آنسة *aanisa* for an unmarried one. When in doubt, أستاذة is always safe.

sections.title: Countries and cities you'll hear often

blocks.text: Egypt is the crossroads of the Arab world, and people from the whole region gather in Cairo. The following names come up in conversation almost every day.

Notice that the word مصر means two things: the country of Egypt and — for villagers and older people — the city of Cairo. This habit is thousands of years old, and Cairenes themselves still say رايح مصر when they mean "going downtown".

items: Where are you from? (to a woman)
I'm an engineer, but now I'm a student.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right nationality form.
Make these sentences negative with مش.
Put the words in the right order.
items: مهندس / أنا / بس / طالب / دلوقتي / أنا

answers: انتي منين؟ — أنا من إندونيسيا، من باندونج. — هو مصري، من الإسكندرية. — أنا مهندس، بس دلوقتي أنا طالب. — احنا مش أمريكان.
أنا مش مصري. — هي مش مدرسة. — الأكل مش حلو أوي. — احنا مش فاهمين. — أسوان مش قريبة من القاهرة.
انتي منين؟ — أنا من إندونيسيا. — أنا مهندس بس دلوقتي أنا طالب. — هي ساكنة في القاهرة. — أسوان بعيدة، مش كده؟
